detailedExplanation: This topic is verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Biology Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and the corresponding AQA GCSE Biology 8461 content.

A cell is the basic unit of life. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic: their genetic material is enclosed inside a nucleus. Bacteria are prokaryotic: they are much smaller and their main DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus.

Most animal cells contain a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. The nucleus contains genetic material and controls many cell activities. Cytoplasm is where many chemical reactions happen. The cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Ribosomes are where proteins are made.

Plant cells also contain these structures, but usually have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole. The cell wall strengthens and supports the cell. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and absorb light energy for photosynthesis. The vacuole contains cell sap and helps maintain cell rigidity.

Bacterial cells have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall. They do not have a nucleus. Their genetic material is usually one circular DNA loop, and they may also contain small rings of DNA called plasmids.
You must distinguish eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells, identify the main sub-cellular structures, and link each structure to its function.

Explain biological ideas as linked steps: name the structure or process, state what happens, and connect it to the effect on the cell, organism or ecosystem. Use precise scientific terms rather than everyday substitutes.
examTips: For a structure–function question, use: structure → feature → function. Example: “A palisade cell contains many chloroplasts, so it can absorb more light for photosynthesis.”
